author: Coningham et al.
asr_identification: the Maya Devi Temple in the Sacred Garden, Lumbini (Rummindei), Rupandehi district, Nepal
evidence: UNESCO/Durham–Government of Nepal excavation of 2011–12 under the Asokan temple (a rectangular brick platform 26 × 21 m, bricks 380 × 250 × 70 mm, exposed by the Japan Buddhist Federation in the 1990s). In Trench C5 at the temple's centre three successive brick pavements bounded by an E–W kerb of large bricks (max. 520 × 380 × 75 mm) run under the Asokan walls, the kerb built into the Asokan foundations; under the lowest pavement a line of six postholes on the same alignment. Radiocarbon from two posthole fills: 799–546 and 801–548 cal BC (2σ); an early cultural layer 788–522 cal BC; OSL from early land surfaces 545 ± 235 and 990 ± 290 BC. So a timber, then brick, shrine stood on the spot centuries before Aśoka.
quote: Not only did these pavements run underneath the Asokan walls, the kerb itself was incorporated into the foundations of the Asokan temple, confirming that it was part of a pre-Asokan brick structure…Radiocarbon samples from two contemporary posthole fills (contexts 553 and 557) provided dates of 799–546 BC and 801–548 BC (Table 1)
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (Rummindei, high) and adds site evidence: excavation shows the shrine at the spot marked by the pillar goes back to the 8th–6th c. BC. The same excavation is already in the study through the 2013 report of the Sacred Garden (coningham2013_sacred_garden); this is the dated argument in print. Grade unchanged (already high).

author: Coningham et al.
name_in_asr: a tree described at Lumbini in the itinerary of Xuanzang
asr_identification: the open centre of the pre-Asokan and Asokan temple under the Maya Devi Temple, Lumbini, read as a tree shrine (bodhigara)
evidence: No structure and no roof tiles in the centre of Trench C5; thin-section micromorphology shows substantial root features in an open space there, with fine organic matter brought in from outside, and pavements kept clean. The authors read the kerb and posthole alignments as enclosing a living tree, compare the bodhigaras of Sri Lanka and the reliefs of Bharhut and Sanchi, and connect it with the tree Xuanzang describes at Lumbini (citing Falk 2006). They do not claim the same tree lived on, only that a tree was kept and replaced at the spot.
quote: micromorphological analysis has confirmed substantial root features within an open environment at the centre of the temple…have enclosed a central tree. A tree is described at Lumbini in the itinerary of Xuanzang (Falk 2006).
note: Adds evidence for the entry's own content: Xuanzang's withered aśoka tree of the birth (無憂華樹) would stand in a tradition of a tree kept at the centre of the shrine since before Aśoka. An interpretation of roots and an empty centre, not a find of the 7th century; it does not move the site.

author: Coningham et al.
asr_identification: the pillar beside the Maya Devi Temple, Lumbini (Rummindei), Nepal
evidence: Recalls how the site was found: unlike Sarnath, Kusinagara and Bodh Gaya, found by epigraphy and by matching the pilgrims' topography, Lumbini was come upon in 1896 by Führer and General Rana, Governor of Palpa, at a mound with a shrine of Rupadevi; the identification rested on likeness to the pilgrims' descriptions and on the Asokan inscription that gives the name Lumbini. No new work on the pillar itself.
quote: Their identification was based on topographical similarities with the pilgrims’ descriptions and an Asokan inscription recording the name Lumbini (Uesaka 2001: 75)
note: Agrees (Rummindei pillar, high: the inscription names the place). Nothing new for the pillar or for the oil river (油河).

author: Huxley
evidence: On Führer's 1891–92 season at Ramnagar: he opened two stūpas and found a reliquary, two Buddha images, terracottas and about a thousand carved bricks. Huxley shows that the Progress Report's proofs were made up: 'inscriptions of the second and first centuries BC' found on the spot and confirming that Ramnagar was the city are not in the Lucknow Museum; the 'Neminatha' and 'Mihara monastery' inscriptions were compiled from Mathura inscriptions in Bühler's translations (Lüders); the sixteen Mitra coins 'under the foundations' are of a kind he had said could be bought from villagers.
quote: First, he invented a geographical pointer confirming that Ramnagar was Adhikshetra. The identification was proved by “inscriptions of the second and first centuries BC” discovered on the spot. No such objects exist in the Lucknow Provincial Museum.
note: Does not dispute the study's and Mizutani's Ramnagar (Cunningham's identification), but removes one support: Führer's 1891–92 inscriptions and dated finds from Ramnagar are fabrications and cannot count as site evidence. The study's note rests on the Pabhosa inscriptions (name only), the survey and the later excavations, so the grade need not change; any citation of Führer's Ramnagar finds should carry this warning.

author: Huxley
name_in_asr: the Dragon Cave described by Xuanzang; cave of Gopala in the hill of Prabhasa
asr_identification: the cave high in the face of Pabhosa (Prabhāsa) hill near Kosam, Uttar Pradesh
evidence: Priority of discovery: J. Cockburn of the Opium Department found the cave and would not tell the Survey where it was; Führer, on his second tour (1886–87), entered a cave in Prabhasa hill by a wooden crib let down the cliff, found an inscription there, and claimed the discovery; Cockburn had the Academy print a retraction and Burgess defended Führer. Huxley takes the identification with Xuanzang's cave as given and offers no evidence on it.
quote: Cockburn of the Opium Department, having discovered the location of the Dragon Cave described by Xuanzang, “distinctly refused to let the cave’s whereabouts be known to any officer of the ASI”. When Führer claimed the discovery as his own, Cockburn challenged him in an Indian newspaper
note: Agrees with the identification Mizutani reports (Cunningham, Führer: the Pabhosa cave) and adds only its history: the finder was Cockburn, and Führer's account of it is contested. The cave inscription is not among those Huxley shows to be forged. No change.

author: Huxley
evidence: Covers Führer's career to 1895 only: one sentence on his 1886 visit to the 'Buddha's birthplace (as identified by Cunningham)', which he rejected, and to Hoey's Savatthi, which he accepted; Kapilavastu and Lumbini (1895–98) are left to a sequel.
note: Nothing on the location of Kapilavastu or Lumbini. Useful only as background on how far Führer's reports can be trusted.

author: Amar
asr_identification: the prominent hill beside Gayā town (Brahmayoni), Gaya district, Bihar
evidence: Amar's field survey (2005–06) looked for Xuanzang's hundred-foot Aśokan stūpa on the hilltop and for the three Kāśyapa stūpas SE of the hill: no archaeological trace of a stūpa on the summit, no Buddhist remains on the hill (the hilltop temple is of the 18th century), no in-situ stūpa base anywhere at Gayā, only pieces of small Pāla votive stūpas among the town's sculpture collections. The Gayā Māhātmya (11th c.) makes Gayāśīrṣa one krośa of the Gayākṣetra and a place of piṇḍadāna at Brahmāyoni. He holds that Xuanzang was probably right and that the Buddhist shrines were displaced between the 7th and 11th centuries.
quote: Whether there was a stūpa at the top of the mountain is not something I was able to confirm during my surveys because there are no archaeological traces of any such monument…But there is no prominent in situ base of a stūpa mound or similar structure. However, it seems unlikely that Xuanzang is incorrect in locating these three stūpas at Gayā.
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani on the hill (Brahmayoni, medium) but gives negative site evidence: a survey found none of the four stūpas the entry describes. The identification still rests on the name and the bearing from the town, so medium stands and cannot rise.

author: Amar
asr_identification: Gayā town, ten kilometres north of Bodhgayā, Bihar; the Viṣṇupada on the Muṇḍapṛṣṭha rock
evidence: Dates the Brahmanical town from inscriptions and sculpture: a centre of śrāddha from the early centuries CE; the first Vaiṣṇava shrine at the Muṇḍapṛṣṭha (the present Viṣṇupada) in the 9th century by an inscription (EI 35, p. 227), with nine Viṣṇu images of the 9th–12th c. in the complex; two inscriptions of Viśvarūpa in year 15 of Nayapāla (c. 1053) for shrines of Gadādhara and Sūrya; 8th-c. Viṣṇu and Balarāma images at Maṅgalagaurī and Rāmagayā. Nothing at the site is as early as Xuanzang's visit.
quote: Based on this inscription, the first Vais. .nava shrine at the Mun.d.apr..st.ha hill – the present Vis.n.upada complex as noted above – can be dated to the ninth century CE.
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (Gayā town, medium). Background rather than a test: Xuanzang's town of a thousand Brahman families is consistent with a śrāddha centre, but the dated remains begin in the 8th–9th c. No change.

author: Amar
asr_identification: the Mahābodhi temple and Bodhi-tree precinct, Bodh Gayā, Bihar
evidence: Sequence of the precinct from the remains: a Mauryan decorated stone slab (the Bodhi seat, found by Cunningham, still at the foot of the tree); a stūpa, sandstone railing and monasteries by the end of the 1st c. BC; a temple-shrine and images from the 4th c. CE; and, from the Mahānāman inscription's gandhakuṭī (CII 3 no. 71), the temple roughly in its present form in the second half of the 6th century, i.e. standing when Xuanzang came. Eighteen early medieval donative inscriptions from the complex.
quote: marked by the Bodhi-seat shrine, the main feature of which was a decorated stone slab uncovered by Alexander Cunningham in the nineteenth century and still visible at the base of the Bodhi tree…the Mahābodhi temple, roughly in its present form, was constructed in the second half of the sixth century CE.
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (the present temple, high; the precinct). Adds a date from an inscription for the building Xuanzang measured; reported from Fleet and Cunningham, not new fieldwork.

author: Amar
name_in_asr: Guṇamati vihāra; Śīlabhadra vihāra; Yaṣṭivana; Kukkuṭapādagiri; Prāgbodhi; the stūpa where Sujātā offered milk-rice
asr_identification: Dharawat; Kauwadol; Jethian; Gurupa (Gurpa); Dungeśvarī; the Bakror stūpa across the river from Bodhgayā (all Gaya region, Bihar)
evidence: Lists the received identifications of Xuanzang's sites round Bodhgayā and adds, from his own survey of 2005–06 (data not yet published), that Dharawat, Jethian, Kurkihar, Hasrakol and Bakror are early historic monasteries that grew in the early medieval period, while Kauwadol, Gurpa and Dungeśvarī look, from surface remains, like early medieval foundations. All have Pāla-period donated sculpture, votive stūpas and shrines; Kurkihar has 93 inscriptions, Dharawat, Guneri and Hasrakol several each. More than thirty small 'settlement-shrines' with Buddhist images lie in the villages around.
quote: the travel account of Xuanzang who has provided details about Gunāmati vihāra (identified as Dharawat), Yas.t.ivana (identified as Jethian) and the stūpa marking the spot where Sujātā offered the Buddha milk-rice (identified as Bakror stūpa, across the river from Bodhgayā).
note: Agrees with the study for Dharawat (08.04.03), Kauwa-dol (08.04.04), Jethian (09.02.02), Gurpa (09.01.03) and Dungeshwari (08.05.03). Differs on one: Amar calls the Bakror stūpa the Sujātā stūpa, while the study puts Xuanzang's milk-rice place (08.06.21) on the west bank (Tika Bigha, low) and reads Bakraur as the stūpa of the fragrant elephant east of the river (09.01.01, medium). Amar gives the current label for the mound without arguing it against Xuanzang's text; the study's reading of the two entries stands, with this noted.

author: Pradeep & Rajani
asr_identification: Vallabhipur (Vala), Bhavnagar district, Gujarat, on the Ghelo river c. 30 km inland from the Gulf of Khambhat
evidence: Reviews the grounds for Tod's identification of Vala with the Maitraka capital: copper-plate grants found NW of the town in the 1900s; Heras's 1930 excavation at Maya-no-khado, on the lowest foundations of a Buddhist monastery 22 feet down, where plates of Varāhadāsa, Dharasena and Śīlāditya were found in situ; the M.S. University of Baroda excavation there in 1979 (three phases, 1st c. BC–4th, 4th–5th, 5th–8th c. CE); Roman amphora sherds and red polished ware near the Ghoda Daman tank (Jairath). On the DEM the town is a mound 15–20 m above the plain, the only one for kilometres, on a palaeo-strandline with palaeo-mudflats and channels to the east, fitting a former port.
quote: It was reported that the Copper Plates of Maitraka rulers Varahdasa, Dharasena and Siladitya were found in-situ during the excavation indicating the presence of a Buddhist monastery as mentioned in the CPGs (Jairath, 1986)…Valabhi stands out as a prominent elevation in the Digital Elevation Model (elevated to about 15–20 m from the surrounding areas).
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (Vala, high) and gathers the site evidence for it: Maitraka grants in situ in a monastery, a 5th–8th-c. phase, and a city mound. Grade unchanged.

author: Pradeep & Rajani
asr_identification: an enclosure round the old settlement of Vallabhipur, with a moat fed by the two branches of the Ghelo
evidence: A crop mark (Google Earth) and soil mark (CORONA, 1970s) ring the settlement; on a field visit in January 2023 the authors found at the mark a raised bank of compacted earth with loose stone blocks and a dry depression east of it, and derelict linear water bodies on the east side, which they read as wall and moat. The present settlement covers c. 1.5 sq. km with a perimeter of c. 4.6 km. A grant of Śīlāditya I speaks of a camp 'before the gates of Valabhi'. No excavation and no date for the bank; dense housing prevented checking the whole circuit.
quote: On reaching the feature a raised surface consisting of structural remains of a wall was encountered (Fig. 9)…Covering an area of approximately 1.5 square kilometres and a perimeter of about 4.6 km, Valabhi is located on the banks of the river Ghelo
note: Adds a measurable outline to set against Xuanzang's capital of 30 li in circuit (大都城周三十餘里): the present settlement is about 4.6 km round, roughly a third to a half of 30 li on the usual equivalents, so either the walled core is not his 'city' or his figure takes in the suburbs with the monasteries. The authors quote his figure but do not make the comparison. Undated; does not affect the identification.

author: Pradeep & Rajani
name_in_asr: the hundred saṅghārāmas of Valabhi; Dudda-vihāra-maṇḍala
asr_identification: mound M (c. 350 × 350 m, SE part of Vallabhipur, round the Darbargadh) and mounds M1–M6 beside Maya-no-khado and the Ghoda Daman tank
evidence: From the 10 m Cartosat DEM: a square mound M with a slight clockwise tilt from the cardinal points, of the size and plan of Vikramaśīla (c. 320 m) and Somapura (c. 300 m), and six parallel mounds M1–M6 in a line whose outline matches the row of monasteries at Nālandā. The grants place the Dudda monastery, a cluster of six to eight houses named in at least twelve of the twenty-six Buddhist grants, 'to the east of the inner part of Śrī Valabhī'. Two readings are offered: M the royal centre and M1–M6 the Dudda cluster, or M the Dudda mahāvihāra with the royal complex and M1–M6 its dependent houses; Pipli, 4 km SW on a palaeochannel, may be the granted village Pipalirunkha. The authors call it a conjecture pending survey.
quote: suggests that the mound M was the capital and M1–M6 was the cluster of monasteries…but, a definitive assertion can only be achieved after conducting archaeological survey in locations identified by the present analysis.
note: Bears on the entry's monasteries (伽藍百餘所) and on Yijing's Valabhi; candidate sites inside the town, from terrain models and analogy only. Xuanzang's one named monastery, the Ācāra saṅghārāma 'not far from the city' (去城不遠), is quoted but not located. No change to the study; worth a line in the note as places to watch.
